Here, we found no evidence for correlation of velocity with Z-score of Ca2+-dependent signal including a cross correlation analysis to account for a potential temporal offset (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of fiber photometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons induced rearing, treading, digging, rapid locomotion, and jumping behaviors.
claims.source: During the stimulation period, a clear shift in behavior was evident in Cre +mice. Photostimulation induced rearing, treading, digging, rapid locomotion, and jumping.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral observation data during photostimulation experiments.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice engaged in significantly more jumps during the stimulation period compared to WT mice (p=0.012).
claims.source: Quantification of jumping revealed that Cre +mice (n=16) engaged in significantly (p=0.012) more jumps during the stimulation period compared to WT (n=16) mice (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data shown in Figure 4C with statistical significance.

claims.claim: During the stimulation period, there was a significant increase in the time spent treading/digging in Cre+ mice (p=0.004).
claims.source: In the stimulation period, there was a significant (p=0.004) increase in the time spent treading/digging, and, surprisingly, during the post-stimulation period time treading/digging was significantly (p=0.014) decreased in Cre +mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data with statistical significance.

claims.claim: During the post-stimulation period, time treading/digging was significantly decreased in Cre+ mice (p=0.014).
claims.source: In the stimulation period, there was a significant (p=0.004) increase in the time spent treading/digging, and, surprisingly, during the post-stimulation period time treading/digging was significantly (p=0.014) decreased in Cre +mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data with statistical significance.

claims.claim: During the stimulation period, Cre+ mice did not engage in grooming, leading to a significant decrease in time spent grooming compared to Cre- mice (p=0.016).
claims.source: During the stimulation period, the Cre +mice did not engage in grooming, leading to a significant (p=0.016) decrease in time spent grooming compared to Cre- mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data with statistical significance.

claims.claim: In the post-stimulation period, Cre+ mice showed a significant increase in time spent grooming compared to Cre- mice (p=0.005).
claims.source: In the post-stimulation period, Cre +mice showed a significant (p=0.005) increase in time spent grooming compared to Cre- mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative behavioral data with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons produced significant aversion at all frequencies (1, 5, 10, and 20 Hz) in Cre+ mice compared to Cre- littermate control mice.
claims.source: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons produced significant aversion at all frequencies in Cre+ (n=19) mice compared to Cre- (n=21) littermate control mice, and higher stimulation frequencies evoked greater aversion (p<0.001; Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by real-time place aversion data shown in Figure 5B and C with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Higher stimulation frequencies evoked greater aversion in real-time place aversion testing.
claims.source: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons produced significant aversion at all frequencies in Cre+ (n=19) mice compared to Cre- (n=21) littermate control mice, and higher stimulation frequencies evoked greater aversion (p<0.001; Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by real-time place aversion data shown in Figure 5B and C with statistical significance.

claims.claim: WT and Cre+ mice explored equivalently, with similar number of entries to the stim side (p=0.41).
claims.source: WT and Cre +mice explored equivalently, with similar number of entries to the stim side (p=0.41; Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5D with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice quickly left the stimulation side, and the average time spent on the stimulation side of the area was significantly lower (p<0.001).
claims.source: Cre +mice quickly left the stimulation side, and the average time spent on the stimulation side of the area was significantly lower (p<0.001; Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5E with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons yielded significant aversion of Cre+ mice compared to Cre- mice in light-dark arena (p<0.001).
claims.source: As expected, Cre- mice show a preference for the dark side of the arena, however, photostimulation of the SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons yielded significant aversion of Cre+ (n=13) compared to Cre- (n=12) (p<0.001; Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5F with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice spent nearly the entire trial in the brightly lit side during light-dark testing with photostimulation paired to dark side.
claims.source: Cre +mice spent nearly the entire trial in the brightly lit side, demonstrating photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons drove avoidance sufficient to overcome a mildly aversive stimulus (bright light).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from light-dark testing.

claims.claim: Time spent in center and perimeter during open field testing were not significantly different between Cre+ and Cre- mice during 10 Hz photostimulation (p=0.19).
claims.source: In the open field test, time spent in center and perimeter were not significantly different (p=0.19) between Cre+ (n=18) and Cre- (n=17) during 10 Hz photostimulation.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from open field testing with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Distance traveled during open field testing was significantly increased in Cre+ compared to Cre- mice (p<0.001).
claims.source: The total distance traveled was significantly (p<0.001) increased in in Cre +mice compared to WT mice (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5I with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons did not significantly alter preference in light-dark exploration test (p=0.68).
claims.source: We found that photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons did not significantly alter preference (p=0.68; Figure 5K) in VGLUT2-Cre+mice (n=8) compared to WT (n=9).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5K with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: A significant increase in total distance was detected during light-dark exploration assay in Cre+ compared to WT (p=0.003).
claims.source: The activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons evoked escape behaviors in open field testing, as seen in Figure 4; similarly, a significant increase in total distance was detected during light-dark exploration assay in Cre +compared to WT (p=0.003; Figure 5L).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5L with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Photostimulation at 10 Hz of VGAT neurons did not drive significant place preference or aversion (p=0.67).
claims.source: Photostimulation at 10 Hz yielded no significant aversion or preference compared to baseline (p=0.838) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-D with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice paused the photostimulation significantly more on all 4 days of operant testing compared to Cre- littermate mice.
claims.source: Analyses of port activations during the 10-min trials revealed that Cre +mice (n=11) paused the photostimulation (reward) significantly more on all 4 days of testing compared to Cre- littermate (n=11) mice (InteractionGenotype x Day p<0.001; Day 1 p<0.001; Day 2 p<0.001; Day 3 p<0.001; Day 4 p<0.001; Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Supported by operant behavior data shown in Figure 6C with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice engaged the active port significantly more than Cre- mice during all operant training sessions.
claims.source: Cre +mice engaged the active port significantly more than Cre- mice (p<0.001; Figure 6D) and this effect was consistent for every training session (Day 1 p<0.0001 = ; Day 2 p<0.0001; Day 3 p<0.0001; Day 4 p=0.0011).
claims.evidence: Supported by operant behavior data shown in Figure 6D with statistical significance.

claims.claim: The time to the first engagement of the active port was significantly different for Cre+ compared to Cre- mice during the first test trial (p=0.046).
claims.source: The time to the first engagement of the active port was significantly different for Cre +compared to Cre- mice during the first test trial (p=0.046).
claims.evidence: Supported by operant behavior data with statistical significance.

claims.claim: During three subsequent operant tests, Cre+ mice were significantly faster to engage the active port after the start of the trial compared to Cre- mice.
claims.source: During the three subsequent tests, Cre +mice were significantly faster to engage the active port after the start of the trial compared to Cre- mice (Day 2 p=0.009; Day 3 p=0.003; Day 4 p=0.034; Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Supported by operant behavior data shown in Figure 6E with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice engaged the active port significantly more than the inactive port on all test days (p<0.001).
claims.source: Cre +mice engaged the active port significantly more than the inactive port on all test days (p<0.001; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by operant behavior data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A with statistical significance.

claims.claim: During progressive ratio trials, Cre+ mice activated the active port and paused stimulation significantly more times than Cre- mice (p<0.001).
claims.source: During trials using a progressive ratio, Cre +mice activated the active port and paused stimulation significantly (p<0.001) more times than Cre- mice (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: Supported by operant behavior data shown in Figure 6F with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice continued to engage the active port throughout progressive ratio trials despite the increasing work required.
claims.source: Examination of individual cumulative active port activation data showed Cre +mice continued to engage the active port throughout progressive ratio trials despite the increasing work required to generate each pause in photostimulation. No breakpoint was observed during the trial (Figure 6G and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by operant behavior data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claims.claim: As behavior shifted from active coping to more passive strategies and greater immobility during forced swim, the Ca2+ signal significantly declined (95% CI).
claims.source: Examining the timeframe around the behavioral shift in each animal, we found that as behavior shifted from active coping (climbing, swimming) to more passive strategies and greater immobility, the Ca2+ signal significantly (95% CI) declined (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 7B with 95% confidence interval.

claims.claim: Hindpaw swimming was accompanied by a rise in the Ca2+-dependent signal across multiple events within a trial.
claims.source: In a 20-s window centered on the onset of hindpaw swimming, we found that hindpaw swimming was accompanied by a rise in the Ca2+-dependent signal across multiple events within a trial (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: A significant rise in the Ca2+-dependent signal from SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons occurred during the shift from immobility to hindpaw swimming or swimming behaviors (99.9% CI).
claims.source: A similar analysis across events in multiple animals demonstrated a significant (99.9% CI) rise in the Ca2+-dependent signal from SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons during the shift from immobility to hindpaw swimming or swimming behaviors (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 7D with 99.9% confidence interval.

claims.claim: Time series analysis of 20 s epochs centered on random time intervals did not reveal any rise in the Ca2+-dependent signal.
claims.source: Time series analysis of 20 s epochs centered on random time intervals did not reveal any rise in the Ca2+-dependent signal (Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: During 10 Hz photostimulation in forced swim test, VGLUT2-Cre+ mice engaged in vigorous swimming and the time spent immobile was significantly less than Cre- mice (p<0.001).
claims.source: During 10 Hz photostimulation VGLUT2-Cre+mice engaged in vigorous swimming and the time spent immobile was significantly (****=p < 0.001) less than Cre- mice.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from forced swim test with statistical significance.

claims.claim: In the post-stimulation period of forced swim test, the time spent immobile remained significantly lower in Cre+ mice compared to Cre- (p=0.047).
claims.source: In the post-stimulation period, the time spent immobile remained significantly (*=0.047) lower in Cre +mice compared to Cre-.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from forced swim test with statistical significance.

claims.claim: In VGAT-Cre+ mice, photostimulation did not significantly increase time immobile during forced swim test (p>0.999).
claims.source: Photostimulation did not significantly increase time immobile (p>0.999).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from forced swim test with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: In VGAT-Cre+ mice, there was a significant decrease in the time spent immobile in the post-stimulation period compared to the stimulation period during forced swim test (p=0.001).
claims.source: However, there was a significant (**p=0.001) decrease in the time spent immobile compared to the post-stimulation period.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from forced swim test with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Food deprived mice spent significantly more time interacting with the food pellet than in the fed state (p<0.001).
claims.source: In the fed state, mice spent significantly less time interacting with the food (p<0.001; Figure 8C) and ate significantly less (p<0.001; Figure 8D) compared to food deprived state.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8C with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Food deprived mice ate significantly more than in the fed state (p<0.001).
claims.source: In the fed state, mice spent significantly less time interacting with the food (p<0.001; Figure 8C) and ate significantly less (p<0.001; Figure 8D) compared to food deprived state.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8D with statistical significance.

claims.claim: At the time of food presentation in food deprived mice, the Ca2+-dependent signal decreased significantly (99.9% CI) but not the isosbestic signal.
claims.source: At the time of food presentation, the Ca2+-dependent signal decreased significantly (99.9% CI) but not the isosbestic signal.
claims.evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data with 99.9% confidence interval.

claims.claim: The change in the Ca2+-dependent signal was larger and more sustained when the animals spent longer interacting with the food.
claims.source: The change in the Ca2+-dependent signal was larger and more sustained when the animals spent longer interacting with the food (Figure 8E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data shown in Figure 8E and F.

claims.claim: During the photostimulation period in feeding test, Cre+ mice spent significantly less time interacting with the food compared to Cre- mice (p<0.001).
claims.source: During the photostimulation period, Cre +mice spent significantly less time interacting with the food compared to Cre- mice (p<0.001).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from feeding test with statistical significance.

claims.claim: During the post-stimulation phase of feeding test, Cre+ mice continued to interact with the food significantly less than Cre- mice (p<0.001).
claims.source: Surprisingly, the decrease in time spent interacting with food continued into the post-stimulation phase, where Cre +mice continued to interact with the food significantly less than Cre- mice (p<0.001; Figure 8H).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8H with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice consumed significantly less food during the 20 min trial than Cre- mice (p=0.001).
claims.source: Reflecting the decrease in time spent with the food, Cre +mice consumed significantly less food during the 20 min trial than Cre- mice (p=0.001; Figure 8I).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8I with statistical significance.

claims.claim: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are positioned as a hub, connecting to areas implicated in regulating stress responses.
claims.source: Thus, SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are positioned as a hub, connecting to areas implicated in regulating stress responses.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the anatomical data showing projections to multiple stress-related brain areas.

claims.claim: Recruitment of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons correlated with active coping behaviors.
claims.source: Here we report SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are recruited by diverse threatening stressors, and recruitment correlated with active coping behaviors.
claims.evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data showing correlation between neural activity and active coping behaviors.

claims.claim: Selective photoactivation of the SuMVGLUT2+::POA population drove aversion but not anxiety like behaviors.
claims.source: We found that selective photoactivation of the SuMVGLUT2+::POA population drove aversion but not anxiety like behaviors.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from real-time place aversion and open field/light-dark testing.

claims.claim: Activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons in the absence of acute stressors evoked active coping like behaviors.
claims.source: Activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons in the absence of acute stressors evoked active coping like behaviors and drove instrumental behavior.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from photostimulation experiments showing jumping, digging, and treading behaviors.

claims.claim: Activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons drove instrumental behavior.
claims.source: Activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons in the absence of acute stressors evoked active coping like behaviors and drove instrumental behavior.
claims.evidence: Supported by operant behavior data showing mice learned to activate the active port to pause stimulation.

claims.claim: Activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons was sufficient to convert passive coping strategies to active behaviors during acute stress.
claims.source: Also, activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons was sufficient to convert passive coping strategies to active behaviors during acute stress.
claims.evidence: Supported by forced swim test data showing photostimulation converted immobility to swimming/climbing.

claims.claim: Activation of GABAergic (VGAT+) SuM neurons did not alter drive aversion or active coping during stimulation.
claims.source: In contrast, we found activation of GABAergic (VGAT+) SuM neurons (SuMVGAT+) neurons did not alter drive aversion or active coping, but termination of photostimulation was followed by increased mobility in the forced swim test.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from VGAT-Cre mice showing no effect during stimulation.

claims.claim: Termination of photostimulation of SuMVGAT+ neurons was followed by increased mobility in the forced swim test.
claims.source: In contrast, we found activation of GABAergic (VGAT+) SuM neurons (SuMVGAT+) neurons did not alter drive aversion or active coping, but termination of photostimulation was followed by increased mobility in the forced swim test.
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data from forced swim test with VGAT-Cre mice.

claims.claim: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons establish a new node in stress response circuitry that has projections to many brain areas and evokes flexible active coping behaviors.
claims.source: These findings establish a new node in stress response circuitry that has projections to many brain areas and evokes flexible active coping behaviors.
claims.evidence: Summary statement integrating anatomical and functional findings from the study.

claims.claim: The functioning of circuits underlying active coping could be key for overcoming anxiety and related disorders.
claims.source: The functioning of circuits underlying active coping could be key for overcoming anxiety and related disorders (LeDoux and Gorman, 2001; Steimer, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on active coping and anxiety disorders.

claims.claim: The neural circuits, cells, and mechanisms underlying active coping strategies remain unclear.
claims.source: The neural circuits, cells, and mechanisms underlying active coping strategies remain unclear (Gross and Canteras, 2012; Amorapanth et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations indicating gaps in current knowledge.

claims.claim: Research on SuM has focused on connections to the hippocampus and septum, while SuM projections to other brain areas remain less understood.
claims.source: Research on SuM has focused on connections to the hippocampus and septum, while SuM projections to other brain areas remain less understood (Pan and McNaughton, 2004; Vertes, 1992; Kiss et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research indicating focus on specific projections.

claims.claim: Connection of the SuM to the dentate gyrus is well described.
claims.source: Connection of the SuM to the dentate gyrus is well described and seen here for the SuMVGLUT2+ population (; Wyss et al., 1979; Nakanishi et al., 2001; Maglóczky et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior anatomical research and confirmed by current data.

claims.claim: The lack of projections from SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons to dentate gyrus is a notable difference from the total SuMVGLUT2+ population.
claims.source: The lack of projections from SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons to dentate gyrus, but not to other structures, is a notable difference (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: Supported by comparative anatomical data shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: Dopamine receptor 2 expressing neurons in the PVT have been implicated in promoting active coping behaviors and may be a potential target of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons.
claims.source: Dopamine receptor 2 expressing neurons in the PVT have been implicated in promoting active coping behaviors and may be a potential target of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons (Penzo et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research and inference from anatomical data showing projections to PVT.

claims.claim: The habenula regulates active vs passive coping behaviors.
claims.source: The habenula also regulates active vs passive coping behaviors, and the lHb functions in aversive processing, making the selective projections of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons to the lHb of similar interest (Andalman et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2010b; Li et al., 2011; Lazaridis et al., 2019; Mondoloni et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on habenula function.

claims.claim: The lHb functions in aversive processing.
claims.source: The habenula also regulates active vs passive coping behaviors, and the lHb functions in aversive processing, making the selective projections of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons to the lHb of similar interest (Andalman et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2010b; Li et al., 2011; Lazaridis et al., 2019; Mondoloni et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on lateral habenula function.

claims.claim: The PAG has been implicated in regulating defensive behaviors and coping strategies.
claims.source: In addition, the PAG, which receives projections from SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons, has been implicated in regulating defensive behaviors and coping strategies (Berton et al., 2007; Tovote et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on PAG function.

claims.claim: A recent study found photostimulation of SuM neuron projections to the septum drove place preference.
claims.source: Photostimulation of projections from SuM to the septum drove place preference (septum), but the same report found photostimulation of SuM projections in the PVT was aversive (Kesner et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: A recent study found photostimulation of SuM projections in the PVT was aversive.
claims.source: Photostimulation of projections from SuM to the septum drove place preference (septum), but the same report found photostimulation of SuM projections in the PVT was aversive (Kesner et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Some neurons in SuM have been found to correlate with velocity of movement.
claims.source: Populations of neurons in SuM have previously been found to correlate with future movement velocity (Farrell et al., 2021)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Recent studies found activity of some neurons in SuM correlated future velocity.
claims.source: These data are in contrast to recent studies that found activity of some neurons in SuM correlated future velocity (Farrell et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Neurons in SuM can release both GABA and glutamate in the dentate gyrus.
claims.source: Although neurons in SuM can release both GABA and glutamate in the dentate gyrus, our anatomic studies indicate that SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons were discrete from GABAergic neurons and do not project the dentate gyrus (Figure 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Billwiller et al., 2020; Hashimotodani et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on dual transmitter release.

claims.claim: Passive coping strategies have been associated with unescapable stress, anhedonia, and depression.
claims.source: Passive coping strategies have been associated with unescapable stress, anhedonia, and depression (Southwick et al., 2005; Cryan, 2005; Knoll and Carlezon, 2010; Ebner and Singewald, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on passive coping and psychiatric conditions.

claims.claim: Defensive burying is characterized by moving bedding forward or backwards often in alternating pattern and is evoked by threatening and noxious stimuli.
claims.source: Defensive burying, characterized by moving bedding forward or backwards often in alternating pattern, is evoked by threatening and noxious stimuli, and is a described active stress coping strategy in rodents (De Boer and Koolhaas, 2003; Castro et al., 2016; Reynolds and Berridge, 2001; Richard and Berridge, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on defensive burying behavior.

claims.claim: Defensive burying is a described active stress coping strategy in rodents.
claims.source: Defensive burying, characterized by moving bedding forward or backwards often in alternating pattern, is evoked by threatening and noxious stimuli, and is a described active stress coping strategy in rodents (De Boer and Koolhaas, 2003; Castro et al., 2016; Reynolds and Berridge, 2001; Richard and Berridge, 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on defensive burying as active coping.

claims.claim: Grooming following acute stressors is a self-care behavior.
claims.source: A reasonable interpretation of the rise in grooming post stimulation is that photostimulation evoked a stressed-like state and cessation of photostimulation led to selfcare grooming, as seen following acute stressors (Kalueff and Tuohimaa, 2004; van Erp et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on grooming behavior after stress and inference from the observed pattern.

claims.claim: Current theoretical frameworks for examining threat responses divide behaviors into innate (fixed) and instrumental (action-outcome) categories.
claims.source: Current theoretical frameworks for examining threat responses divide behaviors into two broad categories: innate (fixed) and instrumental (action-outcome; LeDoux and Daw, 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior theoretical framework.

claims.claim: Behaviors in innate and instrumental categories are mediated by distinct neural circuits.
claims.source: Additionally, stress responses can be divided into active vs passive actions. Behaviors in these separable categories are mediated by distinct neural circuits (LeDoux and Daw, 2018; Fadok et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on neural circuit separation.

claims.claim: Areas involved in responding to specific threatening stimuli drive an innate fixed behavior repertoire.
claims.source: For example, areas involved in responding to specific threatening stimuli (looming threat) drive an innate fixed behavior repertoire (LeDoux and Gorman, 2001).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on innate threat responses.

claims.claim: Suppression of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons is required for feeding.
claims.source: These results indicate that SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons can redirect behavior away from consumption, and suppression of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons is required for feeding, even in a food deprived state.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the finding that activation blocks feeding and Ca2+ signal decreases during feeding.

claims.claim: Animals must choose rapidly between responding to threats and feeding when foraging.
claims.source: Ethologically, animals must choose rapidly between responding to threats and feeding when foraging.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of animal behavior and survival requirements.

claims.claim: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are implicated in control of switching between threat response and feeding behaviors.
claims.source: The findings here implicate this pathway in control of switching between these behaviors.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the findings that these neurons are suppressed during feeding and activation blocks feeding.

claims.claim: Targeting neuromodulation of a circuit able to act across many brain areas may represent a therapeutic avenue for common psychiatric conditions.
claims.source: Targeting neuromodulation of a circuit able to act across many brain areas may represent a therapeutic avenue for common psychiatric conditions, and SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are a newly identified node in critical approach-avoidance circuitry.
claims.evidence: Speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.

claims.claim: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are a newly identified node in critical approach-avoidance circuitry.
claims.source: Targeting neuromodulation of a circuit able to act across many brain areas may represent a therapeutic avenue for common psychiatric conditions, and SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are a newly identified node in critical approach-avoidance circuitry.
claims.evidence: Summary statement integrating the findings of the study.

claims.claim: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons function as a hub with connections to many brain areas to regulate responses to threatening stressors.
claims.source: Together, the presented data show SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons function as a hub, with connections to many brain areas, to regulate responses to threatening stressors (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: Summary statement integrating anatomical and functional findings, illustrated in Figure 9.

claims.claim: The arborization of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons to multiple areas positions them to be a central hub for regulating behavioral responses to threatening stressors by concurrent recruitment of multiple areas.
claims.source: The arborization to these and other areas position SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons to be a central hub for regulating behavioral responses to threatening stressors by concurrent recruitment of multiple areas.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the anatomical data showing extensive projections to stress-related areas.

claims.claim: Activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons may shift how the stressor is processed or approached.
claims.source: The persistent effect of the acute activation into the poststimulation phase suggests that activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons may shift how the stressor is processed or approached.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that effects persist after stimulation ends.

claims.claim: Release of sustained local inhibition from VGAT neuron stimulation leads to rebound activity of output SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons.
claims.source: One interpretation of these data is that release of sustained local inhibition leads to rebound activity of output SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation of the post-stimulation increase in mobility after VGAT neuron stimulation.

claims.claim: SuM may be an important regulator of responses to stressors.
claims.source: The supramammillary nucleus (SuM) has been suggested to be engaged by threatening stressors and has efferent connections to stress-sensitive brain regions and so may be an important regulator of responses to stressors (Canteras et al., 1997; Pan and McNaughton, 2004; Vertes and McKenna, 2000).
claims.evidence: Inferred from prior research cited and the anatomical connections described.

claims.claim: SuM contains a poorly understood diversity of neural populations.
claims.source: SuM has many projections and a poorly understood diversity of neural populations.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge and gaps in current understanding.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons, although aversive, did not generate aversive pairing.
claims.source: These data indicate, surprisingly, that photostimulation, although aversive, did not generate aversive pairing, as found for other brain areas (Kravitz et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that mice continued to enter the stimulation side despite aversion.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons drove avoidance sufficient to overcome a mildly aversive stimulus (bright light).
claims.source: Cre +mice spent nearly the entire trial in the brightly lit side, demonstrating photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons drove avoidance sufficient to overcome a mildly aversive stimulus (bright light).
claims.evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing preference reversal in light-dark testing.

claims.claim: Activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons does not solely evoke innate stereotyped behaviors.
claims.source: Taken together, results from the instrumental reinforcement tasks demonstrate that activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons does not solely evoke innate stereotyped behaviors and can drive active coping in the form of instrumental behaviors.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the operant behavior data showing learned task performance.

claims.claim: Activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons remains salient and motivating through the tested period in progressive ratio testing.
claims.source: This finding indicates that activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons remains salient and motivating through the tested period and that photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA does not evoke behaviors precluding completion of the task.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the progressive ratio data showing continued engagement without breakpoint.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons does not evoke behaviors precluding completion of the operant task.
claims.source: This finding indicates that activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons remains salient and motivating through the tested period and that photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA does not evoke behaviors precluding completion of the task.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the successful task performance during photostimulation.

claims.claim: Recruitment of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons fluctuates with changes in coping strategy during a forced swim assay with decreased engagement of this circuit during times of immobility.
claims.source: These data indicate that recruitment of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons fluctuates with changes in coping strategy during a forced swim assay with decreased engagement of this circuit during times of immobility.
claims.evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data showing correlation between neural activity and behavioral state.

claims.claim: In the context of an ongoing stressor, activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons is sufficient to trigger a change in coping strategy from largely passive (floating) to active (swimming, climbing).
claims.source: These results indicate that in the context of an ongoing stressor, activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons is sufficient to trigger a change in coping strategy from largely passive (floating) to active (swimming, climbing).
claims.evidence: Supported by forced swim test data with photostimulation.

claims.claim: Greater consumption of food is associated with enhanced suppression of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons.
claims.source: Together, the data support suppression of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neural activity during consummatory behavior with greater consumption associated with enhanced suppression.
claims.evidence: Supported by fiber photometry data showing correlation between feeding duration and Ca2+ signal decrease.

claims.claim: Activation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons can redirect behavior away from consumption.
claims.source: These results indicate that SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons can redirect behavior away from consumption, and suppression of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons is required for feeding, even in a food deprived state.
claims.evidence: Supported by feeding test data showing photostimulation blocks feeding.

claims.claim: The forced swim test is increasingly established as an assay of coping strategy with passive and active components.
claims.source: The forced swim test is increasingly established as an assay of coping strategy with passive and active components, and we used forced swim testing in conjunction with fiber photometry to examine if SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are recruited differentially during active (mobile) or passive (immobile) behaviors (Costa et al., 2013; Commons et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on forced swim test interpretation.

results.result: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons represent a distinct glutamatergic population in the supramammillary nucleus that projects to the preoptic area and multiple other brain regions. These neurons are VGLUT2+ and VGAT-, indicating they are purely glutamatergic and not GABAergic or dual-transmitter neurons. They constitute an anatomical subset of total SuMVGLUT2+ neurons with distinct projection patterns, notably lacking projections to the dentate gyrus and medial habenula that are present in the broader SuMVGLUT2+ population.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C18 are well-supported by anatomical tracing experiments using multiple viral strategies (retrograde and anterograde AAV tracing, combinatorial genetic approaches) in appropriate Cre-driver lines with proper controls. The data demonstrate both the molecular identity (VGLUT2+/VGAT-) and anatomical distinctiveness of this population through comparative analysis with total SuMVGLUT2+ neurons. Sample sizes are adequate (n=3-4 mice per experiment) and findings are replicated across multiple approaches.

results.result: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are recruited by diverse threatening stressors including forced swimming, foot shock, and predator ambush. Fiber photometry recordings show significant increases in Ca2+-dependent GCaMP signals (99.9% CI, ~5 standard deviations) during acute stress exposure across multiple stressor modalities, with signals returning to baseline when stressors are removed.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C25 are supported by converging evidence from immunohistochemistry (cFos expression) and fiber photometry experiments across multiple stressor types. The use of both Ca2+-dependent and isosbestic control signals strengthens the findings. Statistical analysis using confidence intervals (95%, 99%, 99.9% CI) is appropriate for fiber photometry data. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6-9 mice depending on assay). The consistency of findings across different stressor modalities strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Activity of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons does not correlate with spontaneous locomotor velocity, distinguishing these neurons from other SuM populations that encode movement velocity. Cross-correlation analysis confirmed no temporal relationship between velocity and neural activity during open field exploration.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by systematic analysis of fiber photometry data during spontaneous movement in two separate cohorts (n=9 and n=13 mice). The inclusion of cross-correlation analysis to account for potential temporal offsets strengthens the conclusion. This is an important control that distinguishes the stress-related activity of these neurons from general locomotor activity, addressing a key confound given that some SuM neurons encode velocity.

results.result: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons evokes active coping-like behaviors including jumping, treading/digging, rapid locomotion, and rearing, while suppressing grooming during stimulation. Post-stimulation, there is a rebound increase in grooming and decrease in treading/digging behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 are supported by systematic behavioral observation and quantification during a three-phase paradigm (pre-stimulation, stimulation, post-stimulation) with appropriate controls (Cre+ vs Cre- littermates, n=16 each group). Statistical significance is demonstrated for key behaviors with appropriate p-values. The behavioral scoring was performed by blinded observers, reducing bias. The pattern of behaviors evoked is consistent with active coping strategies described in the literature.

results.result: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons drives robust real-time place aversion in a frequency-dependent manner across multiple behavioral paradigms, but does not induce anxiety-like behaviors. Mice avoid photostimulation sufficiently to overcome innate preferences (e.g., for dark environments) and show increased locomotion but no changes in center/perimeter time in open field testing.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C43 are supported by multiple behavioral assays (real-time place aversion at multiple frequencies, light-dark choice, open field) with appropriate sample sizes (n=8-21 per group) and statistical analyses. The dissociation between aversion and anxiety-like behavior is demonstrated through multiple complementary tests. The finding that mice continue to explore the stimulation side (similar entries, C36) despite spending less time there (C37) is an important observation suggesting the aversion does not produce conditioned place aversion. Controls with VGAT neurons (C44) strengthen the specificity of findings.

results.result: Photostimulation of GABAergic SuMVGAT+ neurons does not drive place preference or aversion, contrasting with the robust aversion produced by SuMVGLUT2+::POA neuron stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C44 is supported by real-time place testing with adequate sample sizes (n=26 per group) and appropriate statistical analysis (p=0.838). This serves as an important control demonstrating specificity of the aversive effects to the glutamatergic SuMVGLUT2+::POA population rather than SuM neurons generally.

results.result: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons drive instrumental learning in a negative reinforcement operant task. Cre+ mice learn to activate an active port to pause aversive photostimulation, showing discrimination between active and inactive ports, improvement across training days, and sustained motivation in progressive ratio testing without reaching a breakpoint.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C51 are supported by systematic operant behavior testing over multiple days with appropriate controls (Cre+ vs Cre-, n=11 each) and statistical analyses including interaction effects. The progressive ratio data (C50-C51) is particularly compelling, showing continued engagement despite increasing work requirements. This demonstrates that activation of these neurons can drive flexible, goal-directed behavior rather than only stereotyped responses. The discrimination between active and inactive ports (C49) confirms learning specificity.

results.result: Activity of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons fluctuates with coping strategy during forced swim, with decreased activity during passive coping (immobility) and increased activity during active coping behaviors (swimming, climbing, hindpaw swimming). This correlation is specific to behavioral transitions and not observed at random time points.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 and C113 are supported by fiber photometry recordings combined with automated behavioral analysis using deep learning (LabGym) during forced swim tests (n=9 mice). The use of automated behavioral classification provides high temporal resolution and reduces observer bias. Statistical analysis using confidence intervals (95% and 99.9% CI) is appropriate. The inclusion of random time point analysis as a control (C55) strengthens the conclusion that activity changes are specifically related to behavioral transitions.

results.result: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons is sufficient to convert passive coping strategies to active coping during ongoing stress in the forced swim test. During stimulation, Cre+ mice show significantly reduced immobility compared to controls, with effects persisting into the post-stimulation period.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57, C72, and C114 are supported by a two-day forced swim paradigm with photostimulation on day 2 (n=9 Cre+, n=11 Cre-). The experimental design appropriately establishes baseline passive coping on day 1 before testing the effect of stimulation on day 2. Statistical significance is demonstrated for both stimulation and post-stimulation periods. The persistence of effects after stimulation ends (C57) is an interesting finding suggesting potential state-dependent changes, though the mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: Photostimulation of GABAergic SuMVGAT+ neurons does not alter active coping during stimulation but produces a rebound increase in mobility during the post-stimulation period in forced swim testing, contrasting with the immediate effects of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neuron stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 and C73-C74 are supported by forced swim testing with photostimulation in VGAT-Cre mice (n=10-11 per group). The finding of no effect during stimulation but significant effects post-stimulation (p=0.001) is intriguing and suggests potential circuit interactions. However, the interpretation that this reflects rebound activity of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons (C105) is speculative and would require additional experiments to confirm.

results.result: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are suppressed during feeding behavior, with greater suppression associated with longer feeding duration. Food-deprived mice show significantly more feeding behavior and greater decreases in Ca2+-dependent signals upon food presentation compared to fed mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63 and C115 are supported by fiber photometry recordings during feeding tests in fed vs. food-deprived states (n=9 mice). The correlation between feeding duration and signal suppression (C63) is demonstrated. Statistical analysis shows significant differences (99.9% CI for food-deprived, 95% CI for fed state). The use of both Ca2+-dependent and isosbestic signals strengthens the interpretation. However, the claim that "suppression is required" (C97) goes beyond what is directly demonstrated by correlation.

results.result: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons blocks feeding behavior in food-deprived mice, with effects persisting into the post-stimulation period. Cre+ mice spend significantly less time interacting with food and consume less food overall compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 and C116 are supported by feeding tests with photostimulation in food-deprived mice (n=16-17 per group) with appropriate statistical analyses (p<0.001 for multiple comparisons). The persistence of effects into the post-stimulation period (C65) is notable. However, the claim that "suppression is required for feeding" (C97) is an inference from correlation and manipulation data rather than a direct demonstration of necessity, which would require inhibition experiments.

results.result: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons function as a hub in stress response circuitry, with projections to multiple stress-related brain areas. These neurons are recruited by threatening stressors, correlate with active coping behaviors, drive aversion without anxiety, evoke active coping-like behaviors, and support instrumental learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71, C75, C101-C103 represent integrative conclusions supported by the collective anatomical and functional data from the study. The characterization as a "hub" is justified by the extensive anatomical projections (C14) and the diverse functional roles demonstrated across multiple behavioral paradigms. These summary claims appropriately synthesize the major findings without overstating the conclusions.

results.result: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are implicated in behavioral switching between threat response and feeding, with activation potentially shifting how stressors are processed based on persistent post-stimulation effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C99 and C104 represent inferences from the feeding and stress data but lack direct experimental demonstration of behavioral switching. While the suppression during feeding (C62-C63) and activation during stress (C22-C25) are well-supported, the claim about "control of switching" requires additional experiments manipulating these neurons during concurrent presentation of food and threat. The persistence of effects (C31, C57, C65) suggests state changes but the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: Post-stimulation increases in mobility following VGAT neuron stimulation may result from rebound activity of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons after release from local inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claim C105 is explicitly presented as speculative ("One interpretation") and lacks direct experimental support. While the post-stimulation effect in VGAT-Cre mice (C59) is demonstrated, the proposed mechanism of rebound activity would require additional experiments such as simultaneous recording from SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons during VGAT neuron manipulation, or testing whether the post-stimulation effect is blocked by inhibiting SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons.

results.result: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons produces aversion without generating conditioned place aversion, drives avoidance sufficient to overcome mildly aversive stimuli, and does not solely evoke innate stereotyped behaviors but can support flexible instrumental behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C112 represent important interpretive conclusions supported by the behavioral data. The lack of conditioned place aversion (C108) is inferred from continued exploration of the stimulation side (C36) despite aversion (C34-C35). The ability to overcome innate preferences (C109) is demonstrated in light-dark testing (C38-C39). The flexibility of evoked behaviors (C110-C112) is supported by operant learning data (C45-C51). These interpretations are reasonable given the data, though some involve inference beyond direct observation.

results.result: The manuscript appropriately contextualizes the work within established knowledge about stress circuits, active vs. passive coping, SuM anatomy and function, and theoretical frameworks for threat responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C9, C76-C79, C82-C98, C106-C107, and C117 represent background knowledge and literature context supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the rationale for the study and interpret findings within existing frameworks. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations of prior work are consistent with the cited literature. These are primarily MINOR results as they represent literature review rather than novel findings.

results.result: The lack of dentate gyrus projections from SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons distinguishes them from total SuMVGLUT2+ neurons, and their projections to PVT may target dopamine receptor 2 expressing neurons implicated in active coping.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is directly supported by comparative anatomical data (C17-C18, Figure 2). Claim C81 is partially speculative ("may be a potential target") but is appropriately qualified and based on known PVT function from cited literature combined with demonstrated projections to PVT (C14). This represents reasonable inference for future investigation rather than overstatement.

results.result: Targeting neuromodulation of circuits that act across many brain areas may represent a therapeutic avenue for psychiatric conditions, with SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons representing a newly identified node in approach-avoidance circuitry.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 is explicitly speculative about therapeutic applications. While the anatomical and functional characterization of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons is well-supported, the therapeutic implications are not tested and represent future directions. The claim is appropriately qualified ("may represent") but goes beyond what the current data demonstrate. Translation to therapeutic applications would require extensive additional work including disease models and safety/efficacy testing.

results.result: The authors identify and characterize a specific population of glutamatergic neurons in the supramammillary nucleus (SuM) that project to the preoptic area (SuMVGLUT2+::POA). These neurons are VGLUT2+ and VGAT-, project densely to the lateral preoptic area, and arborize widely to multiple stress-related brain regions. Notably, this population lacks projections to the dentate gyrus and medial habenula, distinguishing it from the total SuMVGLUT2+ population.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the manuscript as providing 'solid evidence' and praise the authors for providing 'excellent evidence of the specificity of the function of this neuronal population, both from anatomical studies and from behavioural studies.' The anatomical characterization is not questioned and is treated as foundational to the study's conclusions.

results.result: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons are recruited by diverse threatening stressors including forced swimming, foot shock, and predator ambush, as measured by cFos expression and fiber photometry. The Ca2+-dependent signal increases significantly during these stressors but does not correlate with movement velocity during spontaneous locomotion or open field exploration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers state that the authors 'employ fibre photometry to measure the activity of these neurons during various threatening tasks and find the responses correlate well with threat stimuli.' The evidence is described as 'solid' and the manuscript is noted to employ 'an array of different tasks to provide converging evidence for their conclusions.'

results.result: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons induces active coping-like behaviors including rearing, treading, digging, rapid locomotion, and jumping. During stimulation, Cre+ mice show significantly increased jumping and treading/digging, with decreased grooming. Post-stimulation, treading/digging decreases while grooming increases significantly.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm that the authors 'provide solid evidence from experiments using fibre photometry or photostimulation during threatening tasks that these neurons allow animals to produce flexible behaviours in response to stress.' The behavioral effects of photostimulation are central to the reviewers' positive assessment.

results.result: Photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons produces significant real-time place aversion at all tested frequencies (1, 5, 10, 20 Hz), with higher frequencies evoking greater aversion. The stimulation drives avoidance sufficient to overcome mildly aversive stimuli (bright light) but does not produce anxiety-like behaviors in open field or light-dark tests. In contrast, photostimulation of VGAT+ neurons in SuM does not drive aversion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that the authors 'find multiple lines of evidence that mice find this aversive and will act to avoid receiving this stimulation' and praise the specificity demonstrated by showing 'that activity of gabaergic neurons in the same region does not correlate with behaviours in the same way.' The distinction between aversion and anxiety is implicitly accepted.

results.result: In operant conditioning tasks, Cre+ mice learn to engage the active port to pause photostimulation of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons, demonstrating instrumental learning. Cre+ mice activate the active port significantly more than Cre- mice across all training days and in progressive ratio testing, with no breakpoint observed. This demonstrates that activation of these neurons drives flexible, learned behaviors rather than solely innate stereotyped responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm that the evidence shows 'this neuronal population represents a new node in stress response circuitry that allows the animal to produce flexible behaviours in response to stress.' The operant learning data is part of the 'multiple lines of evidence' that reviewers find convincing.

results.result: During forced swim testing, SuMVGLUT2+::POA neuron activity correlates with active coping behaviors. The Ca2+ signal declines as behavior shifts from active to passive coping and increases during transitions from immobility to swimming. Photostimulation of these neurons during forced swim significantly reduces immobility in Cre+ mice, converting passive coping to active behaviors, with effects persisting into the post-stimulation period.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the evidence as 'solid' and note that the authors demonstrate 'recruitment correlated with active coping behaviors.' The forced swim data is part of the converging evidence from 'an array of different tasks' that reviewers find convincing.

results.result: Photostimulation of GABAergic (VGAT+) SuM neurons does not alter aversion or active coping during stimulation. However, termination of photostimulation is followed by increased mobility in the forced swim test, potentially due to rebound activity of SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons following release of local inhibition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the authors for demonstrating 'that activity of gabaergic neurons in the same region does not correlate with behaviours in the same way,' highlighting this as evidence of specificity. The control experiment with VGAT neurons strengthens the main findings.

results.result: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neuron activity is suppressed during feeding behavior in food-deprived mice, with greater suppression associated with longer feeding duration. Photostimulation of these neurons significantly reduces food interaction and consumption during and after stimulation, indicating that suppression of these neurons is required for feeding and that activation can redirect behavior away from consumption.
results.evaluation: While reviewers do not specifically comment on the feeding experiments, they affirm the overall evidence as 'solid' and note the manuscript 'follows a logical structure and neatly moves through the central story.' The feeding data is presented as part of the comprehensive characterization of this neuronal population.

results.result: SuMVGLUT2+::POA neurons establish a new node in stress response circuitry that functions as a hub connecting to multiple stress-related brain areas. These neurons are recruited by threatening stressors, drive aversion but not anxiety-like behaviors, evoke flexible active coping behaviors, and control switching between threat response and feeding behaviors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that the authors 'provide solid evidence that this neuronal population represents a new node in stress response circuitry that allows the animal to produce flexible behaviours in response to stress.' This is identified as the central contribution of the manuscript and is described as 'important' and of interest to 'neuroscientists across several sub-fields.'

results.result: Background claims establishing the importance of stress response circuits, active vs. passive coping, the role of SuM in stress responses, and theoretical frameworks for understanding threat responses. These claims provide context for the study but are based on prior literature rather than new experimental findings.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the background or theoretical framing of the study. They describe the topic as 'novel' and 'important,' implicitly accepting the rationale and context provided by the authors.

comparisons.comparison: Both strongly support the anatomical characterization claims (C10-C18). OpenEval provides detailed methodological assessment of viral tracing strategies and sample sizes. Peer reviewers describe the anatomical evidence as 'solid' and 'excellent evidence of specificity.' OpenEval also addresses C80 separately (R18) while peer review includes it with anatomical claims.

Both support stress-related activity claims (C19-C25). OpenEval emphasizes fiber photometry methodology and statistical rigor. Peer reviewers note responses 'correlate well with threat stimuli' and praise the 'array of different tasks.' Peer review also includes locomotor control claims (C26-C27) which OpenEval addresses separately (R3).

OpenEval separately evaluates locomotor control claims (C26-C27) as important controls distinguishing stress from movement. Peer reviewers group these with stress activity claims (C19-C25) and find the overall evidence 'solid.' Both support the claims but OpenEval provides more granular methodological assessment.

Perfect agreement on photostimulation-evoked behaviors (C28-C33). Both strongly support these claims. OpenEval details the three-phase paradigm and blinded scoring. Peer reviewers affirm 'solid evidence' that these neurons 'allow animals to produce flexible behaviours in response to stress.'

Both support aversion without anxiety claims (C34-C43). OpenEval emphasizes the dissociation between aversion and anxiety through multiple complementary tests. Peer reviewers note 'multiple lines of evidence that mice find this aversive' and praise specificity demonstrated by VGAT controls (C44).

OpenEval separately evaluates VGAT control (C44) as important specificity control. Peer reviewers group this with aversion claims and explicitly praise that 'gabaergic neurons in the same region does not correlate with behaviours in the same way.' Both strongly support the specificity demonstrated.

Both support operant learning claims (C45-C51). OpenEval emphasizes progressive ratio data showing goal-directed behavior and learning specificity. Peer reviewers include these as part of evidence for 'flexible behaviours in response to stress' and also group with flexibility interpretation claims (C110-C112) that OpenEval addresses separately (R16).

Both support forced swim photometry claims (C52-C55, C113). OpenEval highlights automated behavioral analysis using LabGym and temporal resolution. Peer reviewers describe evidence as 'solid' with 'recruitment correlated with active coping behaviors.' Peer review also includes photostimulation claims (C56-C57, C114) that OpenEval addresses separately (R9).

OpenEval supports forced swim photostimulation claims (C56-C57, C72, C114) with detailed experimental design assessment. Peer reviewers group these with photometry data and find overall evidence 'solid.' Both support the claims as part of converging evidence from multiple tasks.

Both support VGAT photostimulation findings (C58-C59, C73-C74). OpenEval notes intriguing post-stimulation effects but finds rebound interpretation (C105) speculative. Peer reviewers explicitly praise this as evidence of specificity. OpenEval rates C105 as UNCERTAIN (R15) while peer review appears to accept it.

OpenEval supports feeding photometry claims (C60-C63, C115) but notes correlation doesn't prove necessity for claim C97. Peer reviewers don't specifically comment on feeding but affirm overall evidence as 'solid.' Both support the data but OpenEval provides more cautious interpretation of causality.

OpenEval supports feeding photostimulation claims (C64-C66, C116) but questions whether C97 ('suppression required') is directly demonstrated. Peer reviewers group feeding data with overall characterization and find it part of 'logical structure.' OpenEval more critically evaluates causal claims.

Both strongly support integrative conclusions (C67-C71, C75, C101-C103). OpenEval finds 'hub' characterization justified by anatomical and functional data. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'solid evidence that this neuronal population represents a new node in stress response circuitry' and describe it as 'important.' Strong agreement on main conclusions.

OpenEval rates behavioral switching claims (C99, C104) as UNCERTAIN, noting lack of direct experimental demonstration during concurrent food/threat presentation. Peer reviewers appear to accept these as part of overall 'flexible behaviours' conclusion. Divergence in evaluation rigor for mechanistic claims.

OpenEval rates rebound mechanism claim (C105) as UNCERTAIN and explicitly speculative, requiring additional experiments. Peer reviewers praise VGAT control data as evidence of specificity but don't separately evaluate the mechanistic interpretation. OpenEval more cautious about speculative mechanisms.

OpenEval supports behavioral flexibility interpretations (C108-C112) as reasonable inferences from data. Peer reviewers group these with operant learning evidence and affirm 'flexible behaviours' as central contribution. Both support these interpretive conclusions though OpenEval notes they involve inference beyond direct observation.

Both support background and literature context claims (C2-C9, C76-C79, C82-C98, C106-C107, C117). OpenEval notes these are primarily literature review with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers don't question framing and describe topic as 'novel' and 'important.' Strong agreement on contextual foundation.

OpenEval supports comparative anatomy claim (C80) and finds PVT speculation (C81) appropriately qualified. Peer reviewers group C80 with anatomical characterization and don't separately comment. Both accept these claims but OpenEval provides more detailed assessment of speculative vs. demonstrated elements.

OpenEval rates therapeutic implications (C100) as UNCERTAIN and explicitly speculative, noting extensive additional work needed. Peer reviewers don't specifically address therapeutic claims but accept overall framing. OpenEval more cautious about translational speculation beyond current data.
